prime.problem: "Three replicas at 1% each, so 10<sup>−6</sup>" is how most reliability claims are made. It assumes replicas fail independently. Shared power, the same bug, one poisonous input or one config push break that assumption, and then the real risk is thousands of times higher than the arithmetic says.
prime.fits: First concept card. cs-4 multiplied availabilities as if parts failed independently; this card shows what happens when they don't, and sets up why the rest of the course cares about what replicas share.
expect: four shared causes: power, bug, poison client, config
prime.goal: Compute P(all down) with and without a shared cause, explain why extra replicas stop helping, and name which engineering moves shrink c instead of p.

attend: In the formula, which term does each extra replica multiply by p, and which term does it leave alone?
Why does the red row of the nines chart go flat at exactly 2 nines from N = 2 onward?
In the poison-request trace, what does failover do that turns one bad request into a fleet-wide outage?
Why does better hardware lower p but leave the floor untouched?
What does a canary to 1 of 40 servers change: p, c or N?

must: Replicas fail on their own with chance p → all N down together with chance pN → it looks as if more replicas buy any reliability → but only if nothing is shared

Anything shared (power, code version, input, config) → one event c takes every replica down at once → c doesn't shrink with N → P(all down) ≥ c, a floor (0.01000099 at N = 3 with c = 1%, 10,000× the 10<sup>−6</sup> claim)
Failover retries the same request on the next replica → a poisonous input crashes each in turn → for that input c = 1 → more replicas just add steps to the outage

c can't be derived from a datasheet → it comes from how the system is run → shrink it (staged rollouts, separate zones, input validation) and measure empirically (MTTF/MTTR distributions, hours of successful operation)
elevated: Nines = −log<sub>10</sub> P(all down) → each extra independent replica adds log<sub>10</sub>(1/p) = 2 nines at p = 0.01 → with c = 0.01 every row is capped at 2.00 nines, which makes the floor visible at a glance
reference: the Kingsbury/Carly Rae Jepsen quote and the Kreps attribution
the Cloudflare 2019 (27-minute) and 2012 leap-second incident details
the simulation's seed and trial count (10<sup>6</sup> windows, 9,996 all-down)

compress.prompt: From memory, write the formula and then one arrow chain: shared thing → one event hits every replica → floor c → more replicas don't help → attack c. Add one line saying what replication does still buy.
checklist: P(all down) = c + (1 − c)p<sup>N</sup>, so it's always ≥ c
replicas multiply only the independent term
shared causes: power, same bug, poison client, bad config
failover spreads a poison input to every replica
shrink c: canaries, separate zones and power, validation
replication is necessary but not sufficient: it removes the p<sup>N</sup> term only

retrieve.q: Explain why going from 3 to 5 replicas moves P(all down) from 0.01000099 to 0.01000000 when there is a 1% shared event, and what that says about where to spend money.
answer: the extra replicas shrink only (1 − c)p<sup>N</sup>, which is already ~10<sup>−6</sup>
the c = 0.01 term is untouched and is 99.99% of the risk
so spend on what replicas share (deploys, zones, validation), not on more copies

retrieve.q: Walk through the poison-request trace: what happens at each step from a healthy three-replica fleet to zero replicas up, and which component's good behaviour causes it?
answer: the malformed request crashes replica 1's parser
the client or load balancer times out and retries on replica 2 (failover), which crashes the same way
then replica 3: same code, same input, so c = 1 for this request
failover, normally a safety mechanism, is what spreads it; a 4th replica just adds a 4th step

retrieve.q: A vendor quotes "replicated 3×, so 10<sup>−6</sup> annual loss". What two things do you ask for instead, and why is a single average not enough?
answer: the observed real-life distributions of MTTF and MTTR, not one mean
the 10<sup>−6</sup> is theoretical: it assumes independence and says nothing about bugs, ops and monitoring, where c comes from
a young system's c is likely its biggest number, and averages hide rare correlated events

compare.q: That card computes 2-of-3 API servers at 99.9925% using 3a²(1 − a) + a³. Which assumption does it share with pN, what does this card say happens to that number under one bad deploy, and when is the binomial number still fine to use?
answer: one bad config or code push is a shared event: all three fail together, so the true availability is capped near 1 − c
fine once c is small and the servers really differ (separate zones, staged rollouts): then the binomial picks the count

compare.q: In probability terms, what is the shared event doing to the replicas' failures, and why does conditioning on "no shared event" make p<sup>N</sup> correct again?
answer: the failures are dependent: they share a common cause
given no shared event, they are (in this model) conditionally independent, so the p<sup>N</sup> term holds inside that branch
total probability: c·1 + (1 − c)·p<sup>N</sup>, which is exactly the card's formula

predict.q: You add a canary stage that catches most bad pushes, cutting c from 0.01 to 0.001. With p = 0.01 still, does N = 3 now reach 3 nines, and does any N meet R = 10<sup>−4</sup>? Commit first.
predict.answer: N = 3: 0.001 + 0.999 × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 0.001000999, which is 2.9996 nines: just under 3. No N meets R = 10<sup>−4</sup>, because P ≥ c = 10<sup>−3</sup> for every N (N = 5 gives 0.0010000001). Cutting c by 10× bought one nine; adding replicas would buy none. To reach 10<sup>−4</sup>, c itself must drop below it.

apply.task: Modify code/correlated-failure.py: make c a function of how you deploy. Model a push to all 40 servers as c = 0.01 and a canary to 1 of 40 that stops a bad push after it has hit only that one as c = 0.01 × 1/40. Print P(all down) for N = 1…5 for both, and the nines. Then run simulate() with the canary's c and 106 windows.
apply.done: Your table shows the all-at-once rows stuck at 2.00 nines from N = 2, and the canary rows levelling off at 3.60 nines from N = 3, and you can say in one sentence why the canary moved the floor while replicas never did.
apply.hint: Canary rows: 1.99, 3.46, 3.60, 3.60, 3.60 nines (P = 0.0102475, 0.00034997, 0.000251, 0.00025001, 0.00025). The simulation should count about c × 10<sup>6</sup> = 250 all-down windows at N = 3, give or take sampling noise.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that N = 3 falls just short of 3 nines with c = 0.001?
